summary: Describes IBM's SNMP support for SNA APPN nodes, defining management objects for those nodes. It is informational and does not define an Internet standard.

eli5.summary: Some old computer networks use their own special language. This note gives a way to check on their machines using the common Internet checking tool.

subtitle: SNMP management objects for IBM SNA APPN nodes and network topology.

tldr.problem: SNA networks run on IBM systems in parallel with IP networks, but administrators lack a standard way to monitor APPN nodes using the common Internet protocol SNMP.
tldr.mechanism: This MIB defines SNMP-accessible objects for APPN nodes, including node identity, capabilities, port and link-station status, network topology, directory caching, and Quality-of-Service parameters.
tldr.outcome: IBM APPN networks can now be monitored via SNMP agents, allowing administrators to check node status, track topology, and manage resources using standard network management tools.

facts.label: APPN node types
facts.value: Network node, end node, LEN (low-entry networking)

facts.label: Node identifier
facts.value: Network ID plus control point name

facts.label: TG characteristics
facts.value: Bandwidth, cost, delay, security, MTU size

today: RFC 1593 is Informational and has not been obsoleted. The APPN MIB defined here remains in use in organizations that operate SNA networks. While SNA is legacy technology largely superseded by IP, many enterprises continue to run SNA infrastructure for backward compatibility and to support legacy applications. The MIB provides an important bridge for administrators to monitor these hybrid environments using standard SNMP tools.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: RFC 1593 defines managed objects for monitoring IBM's SNA Advanced Peer-to-Peer Networking (APPN) nodes via SNMP. The MIB covers the APPN node itself (capabilities, ports, link stations), the network topology known to network nodes, and administrative information like class-of-service and directory caching. This allows IBM APPN networks to be monitored using the standard Internet framework rather than IBM-specific tools. The MIB does not cover SNA logical units (LUs) or sessions, which are reserved for future work.
sections.eli5: IBM systems have their own networking language called SNA. This note provides a way to look inside those systems and ask what is happening with the network, using the standard Internet language SNMP.

sections.title: SNA and APPN Concepts
sections.content: Systems Network Architecture (SNA) is a networking model developed by IBM, predating TCP/IP. APPN is an evolution of SNA that supports dynamic routing and peer-to-peer communication without requiring a central hub. APPN nodes come in three types: network nodes (maintain topology information and route traffic), end nodes (connect through network nodes), and low-entry networking (LEN) nodes (simplified end nodes). Nodes are identified by a control point name, which is a network ID plus node name pair. APPN uses transmission groups (TGs) as logical links between nodes. Each TG has characteristics such as bandwidth, cost, delay, and security level that drive routing decisions. A link station is the physical or logical connection that implements a TG.
sections.eli5: SNA networks have network nodes that act as routers, end nodes that are computers, and links between them. Each node has a name. Links have properties like speed, cost, and delay that help pick the best path for data.

sections.title: MIB Structure and Groups
sections.content: The RFC defines five major groups of managed objects. The APPN Node Group contains general information (name, type, capabilities), network-node-specific data (gateway support, directory cache), end-node-specific data, port information, and link-station tables with statistics and state. The APPN Topology Group maintains topology data replicated in network nodes, including performance metrics, adjacent node tables, and topology views indexed by node name and by first-route sequence number (FRSN). The APPN Local Topology Group describes this node's local topology and known clients. The APPN Directory Group tracks directory caching and search performance. The APPN Class Of Service Group defines service classes, their names, and which nodes and TGs are allowed to use each class.
sections.eli5: The management objects are split into five groups: node info, all the nodes this node knows about, this node's local knowledge, cached directories, and quality-of-service rules.

sections.title: Node Capabilities and Link-Station Monitoring
sections.content: For every APPN node, the MIB reports the control point name, network ID, block and ID numbers (hexadecimal), type (network, end, or LEN), uptime, and capabilities such as negotiable link stations, segment reassembly, parallel transmission groups, and adaptive bind pacing. For network nodes specifically, it reports support for gateway functions, directory cache, route tree cache, and incremental tree updates. Ports report their characteristics and address information by type (TCP/IP, Token Ring, data link switch). Link stations are represented in detailed tables with per-TG characteristics: source and destination addresses, MTU size, pacing window, effective capacity, per-connect and per-byte costs, security level, delay class, and user-defined parameters. Each link station maintains counters for frames and bytes sent and received, exchange identification (XID) frames, and round-trip delay measurements. Link states (inactive, pending, active) and substates track the negotiation and activation of each link.
sections.eli5: For each node, the system tracks its capabilities. For each port, it tracks what kind of connection it is. For each link, it counts bytes and frames, measures how fast it responds, and tracks whether it is on.

sections.title: Network Topology and Routing Information
sections.content: Network nodes maintain and share a network topology database listing all known nodes and the TGs connecting them. The MIB represents this as a graph: tables of adjacent network nodes (peers directly connected) and reachable network nodes (all nodes in the topology). Each entry includes node name, node type, and fully qualified network name (FQNN). The topology tracks performance metrics including route sequence numbers (FSRNs) that identify topology changes, TG segment characteristics (cost, delay, MTU, capacity), and rerouting weights. A second view of the same topology, indexed by FRSN and node name, supports efficient synchronization among network nodes. The directory group caches the location of named network resources, tracking cache hits, misses, and searches. Class-of-service tables define service modes configured on this node, the names assigned to each mode, and which nodes and TGs are permitted to use each mode, enabling administrators to enforce traffic policies.
sections.eli5: Every network node keeps a map of all the other nodes and the links between them, with cost and speed for each link. Administrators can also say which types of data can use which links, and the node tracks these rules.

sections.title: Status and Deployment
sections.content: RFC 1593 is an Informational RFC published in March 1994 and does not update any standard. It documents IBM's SNMP MIB for APPN as implemented in IBM mainframe and midrange systems. This MIB became a widely used extension to the standard MIB-II for monitoring heterogeneous networks that include both IP and SNA infrastructure. Many organizations continue to operate SNA networks alongside modern IP networks, called hybrid networks, where the objects defined here remain valuable for network management. While SNA itself is considered legacy technology and has largely been superseded by IP-based protocols, many network management platforms include support for this MIB to provide visibility into mixed environments.
sections.eli5: This note was published in 1994 and describes how IBM systems let you check on SNA networks with SNMP. Many companies still run SNA alongside Internet networks, so this MIB is still used to monitor those old systems.

layers.label: Port
layers.detail: Physical or logical interface (TCP/IP, Token Ring, etc.)

layers.label: Link Station
layers.detail: Connection over a port to another node

layers.label: Transmission Group
layers.detail: One or more parallel link stations with same characteristics
